title: Split the Pile
summary: Stampwise's loyalty receipts outgrew the biggest database server money can buy. Split the data across shards — and learn why the shard key decides everything: hot shards, scatter-gather queries and resharding.

goals.text: Explain why replicas don't scale writes, and sharding does
See the cost of queries that span shards
Choose a shard key and handle a hot key
Reshard by moving partitions instead of rehashing rows

steps.title: One leader, too many writes
body: Stampwise runs loyalty cards for supermarkets: every till sale writes a receipt and updates points. Peak load is 48,000 writes a second, and the table is 6 TB and growing.
Read replicas don't help here — every write must still land on the one leader. The biggest machine available handles about 15,000 writes a second. Requests start timing out.

card.title: Biggest machine we can buy
lines: # replicas add reads, but every write still hits the leader

steps.title: Split the rows: range partitioning
body: Sharding (horizontal partitioning) splits one table's rows across several independent databases. Each shard holds a subset and takes only that subset's writes. A shard key decides where a row lives, and a router sends each query to the right shard.
The first idea: shard by created_at, one quarter of the year per shard. Each shard owns a contiguous range, so “receipts from March” touches a single shard.

card.title: Partition by range
lines: shard key: created_at
each shard owns a contiguous slice of dates
= “all receipts in March” → one shard, one scan
# the router keeps a small table of boundaries

steps.title: Every new receipt hits the same shard
body: It's November. Every new receipt has today's date, so 100% of writes go to the Oct–Dec shard while the other three sit idle. Four databases, the throughput of one.
This is a hot shard. Range keys that grow over time — dates, auto-increment ids — always concentrate new writes at the edge of the key space.

callout.text: A shard key is good only if traffic, not just data, spreads evenly across its values.

changes: ~ Shard 4 takes all writes and overloads

card.title: Writes per shard today
lines: # new receipts always have the newest date

steps.title: Hash partitioning spreads the load
body: Instead, shard by hash(customer_id) % 4. A good hash scatters similar ids far apart, so each shard gets roughly a quarter of customers — and a quarter of writes.
Each shard now takes about 12,000 writes a second, comfortably below its limit, and all receipts of one customer live together on one shard: showing someone's points is a single-shard query.

card.title: Writes per shard
lines: # hash(customer_id) % 4 scatters customers evenly

steps.title: Queries without the key ask everyone
body: A store dashboard wants “today's receipts for store 77”. Those receipts belong to thousands of customers, hashed onto every shard. The router must scatter-gather: query all four shards and merge the results.

That's four times the work, and the answer waits for the slowest shard. Range scans over the hash key are gone too. Transactions that touch two customers on different shards need a distributed protocol — slow and complex.

callout.text: For important queries that don't include the shard key, keep a second copy of the data organised by the other key (e.g. a per-store table fed by events).

changes: ~ Router fans out to all shards

card.title: Scatter-gather
lines: query doesn't include customer_id →
router asks all 4 shards, then merges
! cost ×4, latency = the slowest shard
# by customer: 1 shard ✓   by store: 4 shards

steps.title: The shard key is the big decision
body: A good shard key has many distinct values (so data can be split finely), even traffic across those values, and appears in your most frequent queries (so they stay on one shard).
customer_id wins for Stampwise: millions of customers, each a small slice of traffic, and the hottest screens are per customer. Changing the key later means moving every row — choose deliberately.

card.title: Choosing a shard key
lines: created_at  → ranges easy, newest shard melts
store_id    → store reports local, big chains skew
**customer_id → even writes, a wallet is 1 shard**
= pick a key with many values, even traffic,
= and that your hottest queries include

steps.title: One customer bigger than a shard's share
body: Brightmart signs up and gives every employee discounts through a single staff account. That one customer_id produces 16% of all writes — and a key always hashes to the same shard.
Shard 2 now carries 37% of the load. Hashing spreads keys evenly; it can't split a single hot key.

card.title: Writes per shard
lines: # one giant account always hashes to the same shard

steps.title: Split the hot key
body: For known hot keys, append a small random suffix — brightmart#0 … brightmart#7 — so its writes hash onto different shards. This is called salting the key.
Writes even out again. The cost moves to reads: Brightmart's balance must sum eight sub-keys. Apply it only to the few keys that need it.

card.title: Salt the hot key
lines: brightmart → brightmart#0 … brightmart#7
suffix chosen per write, so they hash apart
= the hot account spreads over every shard
! reading its balance now gathers 8 sub-keys

steps.title: Growing from 4 shards to 8
body: Next year's traffic doubles. Changing hash % 4 to hash % 8 would send about half of all rows to a different shard at once — a huge migration.

Better: hash keys into 64 fixed partitions from day one and keep a map of which shard holds which partition. To grow, copy whole partitions to new shards, let them catch up on recent writes, then flip the map. No key ever changes partition.

callout.text: The next lesson shows another way to add servers while moving only a small fraction of keys: consistent hashing.

changes: ~ Half of each old shard's partitions copied over

card.title: Move partitions, not rows
lines: 64 fixed partitions: partition = hash(key) % 64
a map says which shard holds each partition
= adding shards moves whole partitions; keys stay put
! hash % N with a new N would move ~half of all rows
# copy, catch up on new writes, flip the map

steps.title: Sharding in one breath
body:
• Shard when a single leader can't take the writes or hold the data.
  • Range partitioning keeps scans cheap but can create hot edges; hash spreads load but scatters ranges.
  • The shard key should have many values, even traffic, and appear in hot queries. Salt the rare hot key.
  • Cross-shard queries and transactions are expensive. Reshard by moving partitions, not rehashing rows.

card.title: Sharding checklist
lines: shard when one leader can't take the writes or data
range: easy scans, hot edges · hash: even, no scans
key = high cardinality + in your hottest queries
! cross-shard queries and transactions get expensive
= plan resharding from day one
